papers.title: SG-ODOM: Event-Driven Proprioceptive State Estimation with Stability-Gated Contact Updates for Legged Robots
papers.summary: Reliable proprioceptive state estimation for legged robots fuses inertial sensing with kinematic sensing from leg encoders. The latter assumes a foot is stationary during the stance phase; however, physical foot touchdown does not necessarily provide a stationary reference for odometry, particularly during impact and load transfer. Repeatedly applying kinematic corrections throughout the same contact phase can introduce redundant or unreliable information. We present SG-ODOM, a proprioceptive odometry framework that uses stability-gated contact selection to schedule kinematic updates. Following physical touchdown, a stability gate accepts the contact for state estimation only after the foot reaches a sufficiently stable support condition. The resulting validated touchdown event triggers an estimator correction, while additional timeout updates bound the maximum duration of uninterrupted IMU propagation. The framework is evaluated on multiple legged platforms, both quadrupedal and humanoid robots, against representative state-of-the-art proprioceptive estimators. Across the evaluated sequences, SG-ODOM demonstrates competitive or superior estimation accuracy, reducing Relative Pose Error (RPE) by up to 25% compared to the baseline estimator on outdoor sequences from the GrandTour dataset. Source code: https://github.com/ori-drs/SG-ODOM. Video: https://youtu.be/-583_RyuhqQ

papers.title: MetaAct: Self-Evolving Executable Action Constraints for Embodied Language Agents
papers.summary: Self-evolving language agents have emerged as a promising paradigm for continuously improving agent behavior through experience. However, most existing approaches evolve textual artifacts, which can influence action preferences but cannot reliably enforce action admissibility in embodied environments with discrete and often irreversible actions. We propose MetaAct, which shifts self-evolution from textual guidance to executable action constraints by synthesizing GEAR (Grounded Executable Action Rules) from execution feedback. Each rule is represented as a typed specification, compiled into a deterministic guard, and validated offline through trajectory replay without additional model calls or environment interactions. Across four benchmarks, MetaAct improves task performance; on ScienceWorld and WebShop, violations drop from 70% to 0% and 40% to 1%, with score gains of +10.1 and +8.0. Our code is available at https://github.com/BaiCubed/MetaAct.

papers.title: Robotic Reward Models in the Foundation-Model Era
papers.summary: Robotic reward models (RRMs) use foundation models to replace per-task reward engineering with reusable, task-conditioned evaluation. Yet under one name, their outputs answer different questions, from whether a task succeeded to which execution is better. This survey organizes 114 methods into five semantic families by the question their native outputs answer: Outcome, Absolute Progress, Relative, Temporal Value, and Hybrid. Within this taxonomy, we review how model design determines what an evaluator can judge, how raw experience becomes supervision, and how existing evaluation practice tests the result. The review exposes a gap: agreement with demonstration order and downstream policy gains do not show whether a reward tracks task fulfillment. We therefore introduce RRM-Bench-1K, 1,117 real-robot videos of closed-loop executions with task-state and camera-evidence labels, and four contrast suites that separate the credited condition from its usual cues. A unified study of 27 evaluators shows that the strongest final scores rank whole executions well enough for selection and filtering. Dense credit, however, follows the progression of an execution more closely than its task state, and no evaluator signals when the decisive view is missing. How much fidelity a reward model needs therefore depends on the decision it drives. We outline directions from real-failure supervision to metrics that separate task state from chronology, and open-source RRM-Hub, a toolbox in which 14 existing RRMs can be readily applied and new evaluators tested on the same capabilities.

papers.title: CLIFT: Contrastive LiDAR Instance Features for 3D Pedestrian Tracking
papers.summary: A social robot has to keep track of the people around it over time to plan its motion, a task handled by 3D multi-object tracking. For the LiDAR modality, trackers usually sit on top of a detector and link its detections across frames with a separate motion model or re-identification network. We instead show how a 3D LiDAR detector itself can be turned into a tracker by adding an instance-level contrastive objective on its intermediate voxel features. Each embedding is read from the voxels inside a detected box, and boxes are matched across frames by cosine similarity and the Hungarian algorithm, without a motion model. The detector backbone is fine-tuned together with this objective, which learns identity-aware features while leaving detection accuracy essen- tially intact. Because the method uses only the voxel features that Li- DAR detectors already produce, it is backbone-agnostic. On the JRDB 3D tracking leaderboard our LiDAR-only tracker ranks first on HOTA (38.58) and IDF1 (37.99), 13.04 and 9.30 points above the next pub- lished method, and second on MOTA and OSPA. Code is available at https://hermak56.github.io/CLIFT/.

papers.title: AVD: A Multi-Sensor Teleoperated Wheelchair Platform with Safety-Aware Control
papers.summary: Electric wheelchairs predominantly rely on manual joystick interfaces, which present critical barriers to independent mobility for individuals with severe motor and visual impairments. This paper presents AVD (Autonomous Vehicle Drive), a dependable teleoperation architecture for assistive mobility that unifies perception, communication, embedded control, and remote supervision in a single low-cost platform built entirely from commercially available hardware. The central engineering contribution is a safety-oriented design framework: control authority follows a static hierarchy, a manual emergency stop and the occupant's joystick pre-empt remote commands, and the on-board sensing layer has stop-only authority. The compute design partitions primary and safety functions and specifies a heartbeat-driven safe-state transition for the fault cases considered. The sensing stack this framework depends on is characterized against measured data: per-channel acquisition latency, a 2,025-scan LiDAR degradation campaign spanning five target configurations and a control under water mist, airborne dust, and direct aperture occlusion, and attitude measurements across static inclines to 47 degrees. The lowest pooled environmental-condition mean retained 76.6% of the clear-baseline forward-sector yield, and no scan lost the sector completely. A logged vibration-induced inertial dropout occurred while LiDAR and camera logging continued, illustrating complementary channel behavior. The result is a documented prototype and an explicit validation path for a deployable wheelchair implementation.

papers.title: ACiT: Proprioceptive-Prior Action Chunking with Inverted Transformers
papers.summary: Visuomotor policies condition action prediction on visual and proprioceptive observations. While historical proprioceptive sequences carry rich dynamic priors, current methods treat them as equal to high-dimensional vision, causing the proprioceptive signal to be overwhelmed. To identify what is lost in equal-conditioning fusion, we analyze proprioceptive data and find that strong inter-joint coupling is the key action-determining structure. This finding aligns with the neural sensorimotor loop, in which proprioception first forms a body-centered prior and vision is later calibrated via parietal remapping. Inspired by this, we propose ACiT, Proprioceptive-Prior Action Chunking with Inverted Transformers, which reinforces historical joint-coupling as the primary condition with vision as a later calibration. This design is instantiated through three modules: Inverted State Encoding builds a proprioceptive prior via per-joint tokens and inter-joint self-attention. State-Visual Grounding lets joint tokens query visual evidence, making vision goal- and calibration-only. Inverted Action Chunking decodes per-joint trajectories independently. ACiT improves success rates on most LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world tasks, with the largest gains on those that require dynamics and coordination. The same conditioning design transferred to the VLA backbone pi_0-ACiT yields significant gains with better execution efficiency.

papers.title: TaF-Foundation: Wrench-Grounded Cross-Sensor Tactile Representations
papers.summary: Tactile sensing is essential for contact-rich manipulation, yet heterogeneous sensing mechanisms and observation formats hinder cross-hardware transfer. Since physical contact is governed by Newtonian mechanics, we ground tactile representations in six-dimensional wrenches, establishing a common physical reference across sensing mechanisms. Specifically, we pair tactile observations from all sensors with wrench measurements, enabling shared physical supervision without requiring direct tactile-to-tactile pairing between sensors. To support learning at scale, we develop a dedicated acquisition platform and collect over 100 million paired tactile observations and wrench measurements from 24 sensors spanning four families of sensing principles. Building on this dataset, our framework combines sensor-specific input adaptation with a shared tactile encoder. By learning to reconstruct wrenches, the encoder maps observations from different sensors into a shared, continuous feature space grounded in contact physics. To leverage these representations for manipulation, we introduce TaF-Policy, which integrates tactile features with visual observations and robot states to generate action chunks. We evaluate the learned representations through wrench estimation, cross-sensor retrieval, few-shot adaptation to unseen sensors, and robotic manipulation. On the core benchmark, our method reduces single-frame force RMSE by 17.1% and improves cross-sensor retrieval R@1 by 13.11 percentage points over the strongest baseline. In manipulation experiments, TaF-Policy achieves average success rates of 51.33% across three simulated tasks and 46.25% across four real-world tasks, compared with 47.33% and 23.75%, respectively, for the strongest baselines evaluated on the same task sets. Project page: https://mrjiangjm.github.io/TaF-Foundation/.

papers.title: ARMFUL: Learning Whole-Arm Grasp Configurations for Single-Arm Pickup of Large Objects
papers.summary: Many everyday objects, such as storage boxes, baskets, and chairs, are too large or heavy for a gripper to grasp, yet a single arm can still pick them up by wrapping around and supporting them. Such grasps are hard to learn: wrapping motions are difficult to teleoperate, and existing datasets contain little whole-arm pickup data. We introduce WAG (Whole-Arm Grasp Dataset), the first large-scale dataset for single-arm pickup of large objects, with 1.7~million joint configurations across 793 objects. We sample configurations directly in joint space, execute each through squeeze and lift primitives in simulation, and stress-test survivors under active shaking and external forces. To demonstrate the utility of WAG and accomplish the whole-arm pickup task, we develop ARMFUL, a whole-arm pickup pipeline that pairs a diffusion model trained on WAG, generating whole-arm grasps from the object's point cloud, with a motion planner that reaches them collision-free before the same squeeze-and-lift execution. In simulation, ARMFUL reaches 85.4\% lift success on training and 69.9\% on held-out objects, and it lifts the object in 70 of 100 trials on a physical Franka arm across 10 IKEA objects.

papers.title: Learning and Verifying Progress: Closed-Loop Agentic Planning with Progress-Enhanced Execution for Long-Horizon Vision-Language Navigation
papers.summary: Long-horizon vision-language navigation (VLN) requires agents to track instruction progress and recover from local errors before they propagate across subtasks. However, executors trained on expert trajectories encounter policy-induced state shifts during deployment, and their stop signals do not reliably indicate subtask completion. We introduce Learning and Verifying Progress for VLN (LeaP-VLN), an agentic VLN system that couples progress-aware execution with independent progress verification through plan--execute--verify--recover cycles. LeaP-VLN leverages progress both explicitly, through a progress verifier that verifies subtask completion before the agent advances and triggers dual-phase recovery upon route deviation, and implicitly, by co-training the executor on progress reasoning and action prediction to enhance the executor's progress awareness and corrective control. To adapt the executor to this closed-loop interface, we propose a two-stage progress-enhanced curriculum: behavior cloning on expert demonstrations, followed by joint training on demonstrations, expert action corrections, and progress-reasoning supervision. Policy-generated trajectories expose the executor to both intra-subtask drift and inter-subtask state shifts, aligning training with the deviations encountered during closed-loop execution. Extensive experiments on R2R-CE and RxR-CE demonstrate state-of-the-art success rates among monocular methods trained without additional navigation datasets, while real-world experiments further validate the effectiveness of LeaP-VLN in long-horizon navigation.

papers.title: Competent Autonomous Driving Through Fine Tuning Vision Language Action Models with Symbolic Traffic Rules
papers.summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models offer a unified approach to perception, reasoning, and control for autonomous driving, but accurate action prediction alone does not establish compliance with traffic regulations. This paper presents a rule-guided VLA framework that incorporates symbolic traffic-rule feedback into policy optimisation. The framework combines supervised fine-tuning on expert demonstrations with reinforcement learning (RL) refinement using a reward that encourages encoded-rule compliance while penalising deviations from expert actions. Selected provisions of the United Kingdom Highway Code are formalised as executable first-order logic rules using PyReason, covering speed adaptation, following distance, and road-user priority. A frozen vision-language model extracts scene predicates, which are combined with vehicle-state information to assess the projected consequences of candidate control actions. Offline evaluation on held-out data collected in the CARLA simulator compares three group-based RL methods. The results show improvements in both action prediction accuracy and encoded-rule compliance over the supervised baseline. The best-performing variant increases the overall rule pass rate from 92.9% to 97.6%, with zero observed violations of the encoded road-user-priority check in the evaluated samples. These findings support symbolic rule feedback as a means of improving VLA policy alignment with explicit traffic-rule criteria.

papers.title: Instructions Before Actions: Prospective and Retrospective Language Supervision for Driving Vision-Language-Action Data
papers.summary: Driving vision-language-action (VLA) models can accept navigation instructions, yet predicting a driver's trajectory does not establish that a model follows the instruction. We study how driving-language supervision is collected and evaluated, distinguishing prospective instructions issued before an action from retrospective labels written after observing it. We develop ADVLAT-Engine to synchronize spoken instructions, road-scene video, and vehicle trajectories, and compare three navigation apps on 48 replayed routes. On 87 maneuvers announced by both Google Maps and a passenger, the passenger uses more scene-dependent language. We evaluate four open driving VLAs before and after fine-tuning on prospective navigation-app drives. Fine-tuning reduces passenger-drive trajectory error by 23-59%, but instruction effects remain inconsistent. At real intersections, counterfactual instructions reveal stronger responsiveness: fine-tuned Alpamayo~2 Super gains 31 and 18 accuracy points at 15 and 5~m, while Qwen-Drive follows alternative maneuvers more reliably with a discrete command than with a sentence. We additionally collected retrospective annotations from four people for the driving recordings and describe controlled comparisons of annotation content, timing, and downstream learning; those analyses are pending. Our findings separate maneuver prediction from instruction-following and establish a framework for comparing prospective and retrospective supervision.

papers.title: JEPTERA: A Platform Agnostic JEPA-Assisted Model Predictive Planner for Urban UAV Navigation
papers.summary: Urban navigation for Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) requires planning that accounts for environmental geometry, vehicle dynamics, and moving obstacles. This paper presents JEPTERA, a navigation architecture that integrates a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA), Model Predictive Control (MPC), PID control, and a safety layer. JEPA predicts the UAV's motion response to candidate commands for MPC action selection, while the safety layer checks trajectories against occupied space and predicted obstacle motion. Simulator adapters and platform-specific YAML configurations separate the planning core from simulator interfaces. An ablation study evaluated six configurations across three gym scenarios, totaling 180 runs. The complete architecture achieved the highest aggregate success rate, completing 28 of 30 runs. Additional tests completed one route across three city maps without collisions. Separate integration tests demonstrated operation in Gazebo/ROS 2, MuJoCo, and CARLA without modifying the core planning logic. These results support the feasibility of the integrated architecture for simulated urban UAV navigation and its portability across simulator interfaces.

papers.title: Stability Principle Inherent in Wheel Gait of Planar X-shaped Walker Generated Using Constant Torque Drive and Mechanical Stoppers
papers.summary: Since the late 19th century when the first walking toys were developed, it has been known that mechanical stoppers at the hip joint are crucial for generating stable passive dynamic walking. Recent research on passive-dynamic and limit-cycle walkers has also confirmed that mechanical stoppers at the hip and knee joints are effective for generating stable walking motion, but theoretical research on how this mechanical constraint enhances the overall gait stability remains insufficient. This paper introduces a planar X-shaped walker equipped with mechanical stoppers at the hip joint, and investigates the effect of the mechanical constraint on the stability of the wheel gait generated by constant torque drive on a downslope. By simply falling forward while using the stoppers to constrain itself to the target impact posture, the robot can generate a highly stable wheel gait. We divide the motion of one step into four phases, derive approximate analytical solutions for the state error transition function matrix in each phase using a linearized model, and analyze the increase or decrease in the state error norm using metrics such as its maximum singular value. Numerical simulations demonstrate that while two phases are unstable in terms of the increase in the state error norm, the remaining two phases are stable, resulting in overall asymptotic stability.

papers.title_zh: Stability Principle Inherent in Wheel Gait of Planar X-shaped Walker Generated Using Constant Torque Drive and Mechanical Stoppers
papers.summary_zh: Since the late 19th century when the first walking toys were developed, it has been known that mechanical stoppers at the hip joint are crucial for generating stable passive dynamic walking. Recent research on passive-dynamic and limit-cycle walkers has also confirmed that mechanical stoppers at the hip and knee joints are effective for generating stable walking motion, but theoretical research on how this mechanical constraint enhances the overall gait stability remains insufficient. This paper introduces a planar X-shaped walker equipped with mechanical stoppers at the hip joint, and investigates the effect of the mechanical constraint on the stability of the wheel gait generated by constant torque drive on a downslope. By simply falling forward while using the stoppers to constrain itself to the target impact posture, the robot can generate a highly stable wheel gait. We divide the motion of one step into four phases, derive approximate analytical solutions for the state error transition function matrix in each phase using a linearized model, and analyze the increase or decrease in the state error norm using metrics such as its maximum singular value. Numerical simulations demonstrate that while two phases are unstable in terms of the increase in the state error norm, the remaining two phases are stable, resulting in overall asymptotic stability.

papers.title: OrthoMark: Place Recognition with Point-Anchored Orthographic Height Mark
papers.summary: LiDAR place recognition provides the loop closures of Simultaneous Localization and Mapping(SLAM). Perspective from Z-axis, a gravity-aligned scan is an orthographic map of the scene, and a revisit from another position and heading moves this map rigidly in the plane, a motion that a polar Fourier spectrum ignores and phase correlation recovers. Along the vertical, the heights of the returns describe the structures, but which heights are observed depends on the range, because the sensor's vertical field of view cuts nearby structures low; height thus misleads a global key, yet is decisive once two scans are aligned and compared cell by cell where they overlap. We present \method, a training-free method built on one principle: two LiDAR scans can only be compared through features computed from the same geometric surfaces in both scans. \method retrieves candidates with a translation- and rotation-invariant polar spectrum of the bird's-eye view (BEV), 1.9,KB per keyframe, and verifies each candidate by estimating its planar pose through phase correlation and scoring it with \emph{point-anchored height columns}: every BEV cell keeps a 16-bit mask of the heights of its own returns; within a session, the score is weighted by the expected overlap of the two scans' sensing ranges, computed from their distance. We show that this vertical link pays off in verification but hurts in retrieval, where what a height slice contains depends on the range to the structure. For single robot, \method has the highest AP of the training-free methods without 3D registration on the KITTI development sequences; across robots, on all multi-robot sequences, it matches or exceeds RING++ at 1/350 of its descriptor size and closes more inter-robot loops than the learned BEVPlace++ on all tests.

papers.title: Vision-Language Grounded Semantic Navigation for Autonomous Mobile Robots
papers.summary: Language-guided navigation enables mobile robots to interpret natural language commands and navigate toward user-specified targets in unstructured environments. However, integrating open-vocabulary visual perception with classical robotics pipelines for mapping and navigation remains a challenging problem. In this work, we present a complete ROS2-based system that combines frontier-based exploration, open-vocabulary object detection using Grounding DINO, depth-based 3D localization, and semantic mapping to enable end-to-end vision-language grounded navigation in simulation. The system accepts natural language commands such as ``go to the yellow box,'' detects candidate objects from RGB images using text prompts, estimates their positions in the world frame, and generates navigation goals executed by the Nav2 stack. In a Gazebo-based indoor environment with a TurtleBot3 robot, the system autonomously explored the room, detected three of the five target objects, and successfully executed both natural language navigation commands tested, without task-specific training. The results indicate that open-vocabulary grounding models can be integrated into classical navigation pipelines, though performance is limited by detection uncertainty, depth-based localization error, and incomplete exploration coverage. These findings highlight both the feasibility and current limitations of deploying vision-language grounded navigation systems using lightweight, CPU-only architectures.

papers.title: AsymEEF: Bimanual Manipulation with Asymmetric End Effectors
papers.summary: Teleoperated demonstrations are costly to collect and rarely reusable across end-effectors with different kinematics and action spaces. This burden grows in bimanual manipulation, where each end-effector pair may require new data. We present AsymEEF, a framework for executable cross-end-effector demonstration generation and unified bimanual policy learning. Given a small source dataset, AsymEEF transfers demonstrations to heterogeneous combinations of two-, three-, and five-fingered end-effectors without additional teleoperation. Kinematic teacher anchors provide geometric supervision, while sparse real-world X-Calib anchors correct discrepancies in grasp execution. A shared encoder maps wrist poses and actuator states to a morphology-agnostic latent space, and a morphology-conditioned decoder reconstructs target commands. Generated trajectories undergo replay filtering for task-level executability. The representation also supports a unified bimanual visuomotor policy trained across multiple pairs. Across four simulated and six real-world tasks, AsymEEF improves replay success over adapted transfer baselines, achieves a mean replay-valid expansion gain of 16.6 times in simulation, and is evaluated through downstream policy training on real robots. Project website: https://asymeef.vercel.app/.

papers.title: EVIDENT: Evaluating Evidence Grounding in GUI Agents
papers.summary: GUI agents are increasingly evaluated by whether they complete web tasks, but surface success can hide a critical failure: the final answer may not be supported by evidence observed during navigation. We introduce EVIDENT, an evidence-driven benchmark for evaluating whether GUI agents ground their decisions in observable web evidence. EVIDENT contains 220 real-world English and Korean tasks spanning semantic grounding, contextual inference, and visual grounding, each paired with human-curated evidence metadata specifying what must be verified. We further separate surface task completion from evidence-grounded success using three metrics: TSR, ESR, and GSR, which respectively measure outcome success, required evidence observation, and claim-level evidence support. Experiments on commercial and open-source GUI agents reveal substantial gaps between surface success and evidence-grounded success, especially in contextual and visual tasks. These results show that current evaluations can overestimate agent reliability and highlight the need to assess not only whether agents answer, but whether they verify.

papers.title: Lift, See, Act: Hierarchical Robot Policy Pretraining with 3D Foundation Models
papers.summary: Robot policy pretraining based on human videos is crucial for improving the policy's generalization ability. One main challenge for this task is the lack of explicit action-relevant representations in such unlabeled data. Recent works tend to estimate 3D hand motion trajectories from videos using 3D foundation models (3D FMs). However, they keep solely the sparse trajectories as supervision, ignoring the rich, fine-grained information produced during the trajectory extraction process. To address this issue, we propose LSA, a hierarchical robot policy pretraining framework that includes three phases: Lift, See, and Act. Specifically, the Lift phase elevates 2D video observations into dense 3D representations by adaptively aligning features in the policy's shallow layers with the intermediate representations extracted from multiple 3D FMs. Building upon these lifted representations, the See phase equips the policy with explicit geometric and interactive awareness through dual guidance. It introduces depth-map reconstruction to help the model comprehend 3D spatial layouts and utilizes hand region cues to explicitly supervise the encoder's attention toward task-relevant interaction hotspots. Empowered by the dense 3D representation learning and precise spatial guidance, our policy achieves robust and accurate robotic manipulation in the Act phase. Extensive experiments on diverse simulation and real-world tasks demonstrate that LSA significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art approaches. The project page is available at: https://yiyuan00.github.io/Lift-See-Act.

papers.title: ReRead: Wrong Predictions, Useful Representations - Correcting Frozen Robot Policies by Re-reading Their Own Representations
papers.summary: When a pretrained robot policy fails on challenging tasks, common remedies include retraining the backbone, adding an external visual encoder, or introducing a memory module. We argue that wrong predictions do not imply wrong representations: a policy can retain the required information yet fail to read it out as the correct action. To test this view, we propose ReRead: with the backbone frozen, a corrector re-reads the current and two previous caches to predict an action residual. The corrector sees no images, is trained solely on offline demonstrations from all 50 RoboTwin 2.0 tasks, and adds only 4.17% latency. Ablations and interventions show that the correction relies on the backbone's own representations: none of four external visual encoders adds further gain, and swapping in past caches from other trajectories sharply increases action error. On the 11 hardest RoboTwin 2.0 tasks, ReRead improves the success rates of LingBot-VLA, $π_{0.5}$, and Fast-WAM by 23.45, 13.09, and 8.00 percentage points, respectively. In paired evaluation on all 50 tasks, it raises Fast-WAM's average success rate from 90.73% to 92.66%. On a Flexiv dual-arm robot, it raises success on a phase-ambiguous task from 0% to 36%.

papers.title: Stochastic Self-Distillation for Flow-Based Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.summary: Flow-based vision-language-action (VLA) models achieve strong performance in robotics through imitation learning, yet fine-tuning them with on-policy reinforcement learning (RL) is limited. In group-based RL methods like Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), every rollout step requires multi-step ODE integration, and the sampler's limited stochasticity leads to rollout groups with low variance. We propose VLA-SSD, which addresses both high inference latency and limited stochasticity. In particular, our method self-distills a pretrained flow-matching action head into a stochastic one-step policy by conditioning a single-jump generator on a Brownian path. We derive a conditional action density via our stochastic one-step policy, enabling efficient post-training via likelihood-ratio RL algorithms. We show that distilling VLA-SSD from the $π_0$ VLA reduces the action head's forward-pass time by a factor of 7.7, at the cost of a 5.5% relative decrease in the success rate on the LIBERO benchmark. However, by leveraging the increased sample diversity of VLA-SSD during group generation, post-training a $π_{0.5}$ VLA using GRPO yields a 20.6% relative improvement.

papers.title: XMimic and XSoma: Learning Humanoid Motion Tracking and Locomotion in Under a Minute
papers.summary: We present XMimic and XSoma, which learn humanoid motion tracking and locomotion on rough terrain in under a minute of training. Both follow SuperMimic, which learns a world model of the robot and optimizes the policy with analytic gradients through short rollouts imagined in this model. Existing implementations of this method do not make use of larger GPUs, as every training iteration is a long chain of small GPU operations that run one after another. XMimic and XSoma therefore shorten this chain and run the steps of every iteration at the same time on up to four GPUs. We compile the complete training loop with JAX, including the MuJoCo Warp simulator. For locomotion, XSoma leaves only the dynamics of the robot to the world model and computes everything else exactly, including the terrain height under the feet. It learns with a horizon of one second and without a critic. On four H100 GPUs, XMimic learns to track all 40 LAFAN1 clips with the Unitree G1 in 0.86 minutes, 3.7 times faster than BlinkMimic on one GPU. XSoma reaches the tracking target that Holosoma's tests set for FastSAC in 0.77 minutes, 12.3 times faster than FastSAC on one GPU, while needing only an eighth of its environment steps.

papers.title: UrbanTwin Sim2Real LiDAR Challenge 2026: Site-Calibrated Synthetic Data and Multi-Detector Fusion for Roadside 3D Detection
papers.summary: This report summarizes the work submitted by team arnav007 (submission ID 1054222) for the UrbanTwin Sim2Real LiDAR Challenge (V2X-Real track) at the IEEE BigData Cup 2026. The primary objective is to train 3D detectors for vehicles, pedestrians, and trucks using only synthetic roadside LiDAR data, and to generate synthetic scans that are realistic enough to be indistinguishable from real ones. A CARLA based pipeline is developed and calibrated to the fixed sensor site, accurately modeling the range image, including no-return beams, based on unlabelled real development scans. A combined inference detector, using multiple 3D detectors (VoxelNeXt, PV-RCNN, and SECOND) trained exclusively on synthetic data, is also proposed. Each scan is aligned to the synthetic ground plane and processed through the detectors at multiple ground heights. The resulting bounding boxes are fused using bird's-eye view (BEV) clustering, followed by class-specific post-processing to refine heading, box size, and filter low-confidence detections. The final submission achieved a combined score of 0.8947. The ablation study shows that per-scan ground leveling more than doubled the real-scan mAP, while fusing boxes across different heights and models further improved performance.

papers.title: Fuzzy Explainable Continual Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning for Robotic Navigation
papers.summary: Continual robot navigation requires reinforcement learning policies to continuously adapt to new environments while retaining previously acquired knowledge. Meanwhile, explainable reinforcement learning aims to learn meaningful behavioral representations through policy interaction. However, these objectives are inherently conflicting, as continual learning emphasizes policy stability whereas explainable behavior learning requires adaptive exploration. Existing methods rarely address both simultaneously. To resolve this issue, this paper proposes a Fuzzy Explainable Continual Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning (FECHRL) method. A two-stage behavior cloning strategy is introduced to balance rapid policy adaptation and explainable behavior evolution by progressively transitioning from strong imitation guidance to autonomous reinforcement learning. Furthermore, a fuzzy critic based on a Takagi--Sugeno fuzzy inference system is proposed to alleviate value extrapolation errors during the transition between imitation-guided learning and autonomous exploration, thereby improving continual training stability. Experimental results on sequential multi-scenario navigation tasks demonstrate that the proposed method effectively unifies continual learning capability and policy explainability within a single reinforcement learning framework, achieving stable knowledge retention and meaningful behavioral explanation.

papers.title: Making Koopman Control Guarantees Hold on Robots
papers.summary: A Koopman controller can stabilize its learned latent-space linear model yet fail to stabilize the nonlinear plant. The learned model propagates predictions in latent space, while the deployed controller repeatedly re-encodes the measured physical state. We show that nominal closed-loop stability transfers to the nonlinear plant when the learned and true closed-loop dynamics agree to first order on the embedding's tangent space at the target. We derive a robustness margin for approximate matching and show that a stable open-loop latent model cannot exactly match an unstable equilibrium. We introduce Tangent-Invariant Koopman (TIK), which estimates a local plant linearization from offline transitions and enforces first-order matching to this estimate. TIK recovers the fitted LQR gain at the target, while a bilinear predictor captures state-dependent actuation during large maneuvers. Across four simulated unstable benchmarks, all 40 Standard Koopman controllers have stable latent closed loops, but their deployed nonlinear systems are locally unstable. In contrast, all 40 TIK controllers locally stabilize their respective nonlinear plants. An offline stability test using empirical curvature estimates identifies stable TIK controllers on two cart-pole systems, but is inconclusive under high noise. Under explicit model-error and curvature bounds, an invariant terminal set guarantees constraint satisfaction after entry under local feedback. TIK achieves 88\% constrained cart-pole swing-up success with a 0.25 ms planning budget and controls simulated seven-joint arms within 1-5 ms per step.

papers.title: "Can a Robot Really Care About Me?" How Perceiving a Tutor as Human or AI Affects Computer Science Students' Attitudes and Experiences
papers.summary: Conversational artificial intelligence can reproduce many instructional and social behaviors of human tutors, but students may interpret those behaviors differently depending on who they believe is providing them. We examined how perceived tutor identity shapes students' evaluations of instructional feedback, satisfaction of psychological needs according to Self-Determination Theory, and their communication strategies with tutors. In a within-subjects Wizard-of-Oz study, 27 introductory computer science students completed two text-based tutoring sessions involving Python code-explanation problems. Participants were told one tutor was human and the other was AI, although the same human provided feedback in both conditions. We found participants evaluated both tutors favorably and reported few consistent differences in the instructional value of the feedback. However, participants frequently questioned whether AI could genuinely care about them, which corresponded with the human tutor having higher scores of relatedness need satisfaction. Human presence offered connection and accountability for some participants but introduced anxiety in others. Participants also reported communicating more casually with the human tutor and more explicitly with the AI tutor. These findings suggest complementary roles for human and AI tutoring and highlight the importance of considering psychological needs alongside instructional quality.

papers.title: Adaptive Koopman Predictive Control without Persistent Excitation via Matrix Normal Invariant Priors
papers.summary: Finite-dimensional Koopman models are increasingly used in predictive control, but their accuracy remains limited by truncation errors and offline identification data. Adaptive Koopman predictive control promises to address this limitation, but typically requires closed-loop persistent excitation (PE). Since this is difficult to achieve in practice, in this paper we develop an adaptive generalized Koopman (GeKo) predictive controller that does not require PE. To this end, we formulate a recursive matrix regression in fixed lifted coordinates that extends the Kalman filter with back-to-the-prior forgetting to matrix-valued operators and uses a matrix normal invariant prior, centered at the operator identified offline. For any regressor sequence, and thus under any feedback law, we prove that the covariance remains between two multiples of the prior covariance and that the estimation error is input-to-state stable. papers.title_zh: Adaptive Koopman Predictive Control without Persistent Excitation via Matrix Normal Invariant Priors
papers.summary_zh: Finite-dimensional Koopman models are increasingly used in predictive control, but their accuracy remains limited by truncation errors and offline identification data. Adaptive Koopman predictive control promises to address this limitation, but typically requires closed-loop persistent excitation (PE). Since this is difficult to achieve in practice, in this paper we develop an adaptive generalized Koopman (GeKo) predictive controller that does not require PE. To this end, we formulate a recursive matrix regression in fixed lifted coordinates that extends the Kalman filter with back-to-the-prior forgetting to matrix-valued operators and uses a matrix normal invariant prior, centered at the operator identified offline. For any regressor sequence, and thus under any feedback law, we prove that the covariance remains between two multiples of the prior covariance and that the estimation error is input-to-state stable. On an academic example, a differential-drive robot and a power system with plant changes and little excitation, the invariant-prior estimator yields the lowest overall tracking error among the compared estimators and prevents covariance windup.
